concept.name: Estimator efficiency
concept.definition: A measure of the quality of an estimator based on its variance: a more efficient estimator achieves the same precision with fewer observations. An unbiased estimator is called efficient if its variance attains the Cramer-Rao lower bound, the smallest variance any unbiased estimator can have.
concept.intuition: Given two honest ways to estimate the same thing, the efficient one wastes less data - its estimates bounce around the truth less, so you need a shorter track record to be sure.
concept.mechanics: For unbiased estimators, efficiency of T is the Cramer-Rao bound (reciprocal of the Fisher information) divided by Var(T), so e(T) <= 1; relative efficiency of two estimators is the ratio of their variances and can be read as the ratio of sample sizes needed for equal precision. Asymptotically, efficient estimators are consistent, approximately normal, and have variance no worse than any rival.
concept.formula: e(T) = [1 / I(θ)] / Var(T) <= 1, where I(θ) is the Fisher information of the sample; relative efficiency of T1 vs T2 = Var(T2)/Var(T1). Example: for normal data the sample mean is efficient, while the sample median has asymptotic relative efficiency 2/pi ~ 0.64.
concept.failure_modes: Efficiency is distribution-specific: the sample mean is efficient for normal data but highly inefficient for heavy-tailed or contaminated data, where robust estimators (median, trimmed mean) do better. Optimizing efficiency under a wrong model can therefore amplify estimation error precisely when tails matter.
concept.misconceptions: Most efficient is not the same as best in practice: an efficient estimator can be fragile to outliers, so a slightly less efficient robust estimator may be preferable for financial returns. Efficiency also concerns variance, not bias - an efficient biased estimator may beat the efficient unbiased one on mean squared error.
concept.example: For Gaussian data, estimating the center with the sample median instead of the mean requires about pi/2 ~ 57% more observations to reach the same standard error - the price of the median's robustness.
